p.x:
My dad has an old blue car. He bought it twenty years ago, and it's still working! It has four big wheels and comfortable seats. The horn is very loud: when my dad uses it, everyone jumps!
We keep the car in the garage next to our house. Every Saturday, my dad washes it and checks the petrol tank. He always tells us to look in the mirror before we open the door, because motorbikes come past very fast.
When I ride my bike to school, I wear a helmet, and I always stop at the traffic lights. My dad says I can learn to drive when I'm eighteen. I can't wait!

Getting a driving licence in Thailand is not very difficult, but driving safely takes practice. First, you need to pass a written test about road signs and rules. Then you take a practical test, where you show that you can drive forwards, reverse and park.
Driving teachers say beginners often make the same mistakes. Some forget to fasten their seatbelt or to check their mirrors. Others don't indicate before they turn at a junction, or they brake too late. Keep both hands on the steering wheel, and don't change gear while you're turning. On a roundabout, give way to cars that are already on it.
On the motorway, you must follow the speed limit, and on some roads you need to pay a toll. Never overtake on a bend, and always stop for people at a pedestrian crossing. If you park in the wrong place, you'll get a parking ticket!
Modern cars have many safety features. A warning light on the dashboard tells you when something is wrong, and airbags protect you in an accident. Many people now drive hybrid cars, which use both petrol and electricity. Traffic jams are a big problem in Bangkok, so be patient, and keep your windscreen clean so you can see clearly.

p.t: Why Do Good People Drive Badly?
p.x:
Road accidents kill more than a million people worldwide each year, and Thailand has one of the highest road death rates in Asia. Most collisions are caused not by mechanical failure but by human behaviour.
Psychologists have identified several reasons why otherwise sensible people become reckless behind the wheel. One is the feeling of anonymity: inside a car, drivers feel separated from others and may behave in ways they never would face to face. Minor frustrations, such as a slow vehicle or a driver who fails to indicate, can trigger road rage, with drivers honking aggressively, tailgating or even getting out of their cars to confront others.
Another factor is overconfidence. Surveys consistently show that most drivers believe they are better than average, which is statistically impossible. This confidence may lead them to ignore their blind spot when changing lanes or to drive after drinking, believing they will not be caught. Random breathalyser tests have proved effective in many countries precisely because they change this calculation.
Some solutions are technological. Modern vehicles with hundreds of horsepower now come equipped with systems that brake automatically. Others are social: campaigns that encourage people to carpool reduce the number of vehicles on the road, while also cutting costs. Since cars depreciate rapidly and running costs rise with mileage, sharing a car is often good for both safety and the wallet.
